title: the Vishnu Purana (selections)
tomorrow: the worst age of the world is the best one? who says that?

segments.voice: Yesterday, more of the Vishnu Purana, the book these days have been dipping into one story at a time. Today's story starts in the middle of an evening.

The phone says nine. You look again and it says one in the morning, and nothing in between felt like four hours. The Vishnu Purana has a sage this happens to, on a much bigger scale. His name is Kandu. One evening he jumps up in a hurry: the sun is going down, and it's time for his evening prayers by the river. The woman he lives with, Pramlocha, watches him go and stops him with one question. Evening prayers? For which evening?
screen: `NINE O'CLOCK. THEN ONE.` → `A SAGE JUMPS UP AT SUNSET.` → `FOR WHICH EVENING?`

segments.voice: Here's how he got there. Kandu was a sage of great tapas, the heat of hard practice, living by the river Gomati. Indra, king of the gods, was uneasy at that much power, so he sent Pramlocha, a dancer of heaven, to break Kandu's concentration. It worked. The two of them went to live in a lovely valley, and the days were sweet. Now and then she asked to go back to heaven, and each time he asked her to stay a little longer. Then that evening. When he insists the day is ending, she tells him the truth: by her count, more than nine hundred years have gone by. Every evening ran into the next, and he never noticed the turning. The text lets him feel the full weight of it. He's shaken, and his sharpest words are for himself: all that practice, spent. He sends her away and goes back to the austerities he left. Some readers hear a warning about sweetness, how it can swallow a life. Others hear something smaller and sharper: Kandu never chose to give up nine centuries. He just stopped counting. Nothing in the story is wicked. The valley was lovely. The trouble was that one evening never ended and he never looked up.
screen: `TAPAS BY THE RIVER GOMATI.` · `SENT BY INDRA: PRAMLOCHA.` · `STAY A LITTLE LONGER.` · `NINE HUNDRED YEARS, ONE EVENING.` · then, large: `HE JUST STOPPED COUNTING.`

segments.voice: Find anything that shows time passing, a clock with a second hand, the timer on your phone, or just the rise and fall of your own chest, and watch it. Don't do anything about it. Simply let yourself notice each moment as it turns into the next.
The Vishnu Purana. Today's story from it: Kandu, the sage whose single evening lasted centuries.
Your line: the Vishnu Purana, selections. The valley was lovely; he just stopped counting. See you tomorrow.

original.note: Sanskrit: heat, and the hard practice that builds it. Kandu's tapas is what made Indra uneasy.

chat.meaning: Kandu's valley wasn't wicked; the trouble was he never looked up. Joy is fine; losing count of time is the slip.

notes: 2026-10-14 recipe v3 (story shape). Written fresh: no earlier draft of this day was on disk, and days 1507–1512 were not on disk either, so the review stays general ('more of the Vishnu Purana'). If 1507–1512 already told Kandu, swap for another Vishnu Purana story.

Kandu and Pramlocha follow Vishnu Purana 1.15 (Wilson 1840 numbers the years as nine hundred and seven years, six months and three days). The script says 'more than nine hundred years' and 'centuries'; confirm against the critical text.

Kandu's self-reproach and sending her away: the text has him blame his own lost penance; confirm the phrasing 'his sharpest words are for himself'. Indra's motive (uneasy at his power) and her requests to return, each met with 'stay a little longer', follow Wilson; confirm.
Trapdoor: Marisha, born of the sweat Pramlocha wiped on the trees, marries the Prachetasas and is the mother of Daksha (VP 1.15); confirm.
